title: Ornamental Plant Production Principles and Cultivation Practices

lessons.title: How ornamental plants grow
lessons.html:
The basics every nursery supervisor must know

An ornamental nursery grows plants that people buy for their looks: bedding plants such as petunias and marigolds, shrubs such as plumbago and duranta, trees, succulents, indigenous plants like agapanthus and strelitzia, and indoor foliage plants. Whatever the plant, it needs the same things to grow well: light, water, air, nutrients, a root medium and the right temperature. When one of these is wrong, growth slows and quality drops.

What the plant needs

  • Light drives photosynthesis, where leaves turn carbon dioxide and water into sugars. Too little light gives long, weak, pale plants. Too much can scorch shade plants such as ferns and clivias.
  • Water carries nutrients and keeps cells firm. Overwatering drowns roots because air is pushed out of the medium; underwatering causes wilting and leaf drop.
  • Air in the root zone lets roots breathe. A good growing medium has open pores that hold both air and water.
  • Nutrients come from the medium and from fertiliser. Nitrogen (N) supports leaf growth, phosphorus (P) supports roots and flowering, and potassium (K) supports strength and disease resistance.
  • Temperature controls how fast plants grow. Most bedding plants grow best in mild conditions; frost in the Highveld winter can kill tender stock left outside.

Plant life stages in the nursery

Most nursery plants move through clear stages: seed or cutting, rooting or germination, young plant (plug or liner), growing on in a bag or pot, hardening off, and finally a saleable plant. Each stage has different needs. A plug tray of seedlings needs gentle misting and protection, while a 20-litre tree in the open needs full sun and deep watering.

As a supervisor you must recognise what a healthy plant looks like at each stage: good colour, compact shape, white healthy roots, no pests, and the right size for the order. Learning to read plants daily is the first skill of good production.

lessons.title: Propagation methods
lessons.html:
Making new plants

Propagation is how the nursery makes new plants. The method chosen depends on the plant, the cost and how true to type the plant must be.

Seed propagation

Seed is cheap and quick for large numbers of bedding plants, vegetables and many indigenous species. Seed is sown in trays or plug trays filled with a fine, clean seedling mix. Key points: use fresh, labelled seed, sow at the depth on the packet, keep the medium moist but not wet, and keep temperature steady. Record the sowing date and the batch so that germination can be checked.

Vegetative propagation

Vegetative methods copy the parent plant exactly, so flower colour and form stay the same.

  • Cuttings: tip, softwood, semi-hardwood or hardwood pieces of stem are taken from healthy stock plants, often dipped in rooting hormone, and placed in a mist or fog house until roots form. Pelargoniums, lavender and many shrubs are grown this way.
  • Division: clumping plants such as agapanthus, dietes and many grasses are split into smaller pieces, each with roots and shoots.
  • Layering: a stem is made to root while still attached to the parent.
  • Grafting and budding: a piece of the wanted plant is joined to a strong rootstock, common with roses and some fruit trees.
  • Tissue culture: plants are multiplied in a laboratory and arrive as small plantlets that must be weaned carefully.

Hygiene in propagation

Young plants are easily killed by fungal diseases such as damping-off. Keep benches, trays and tools clean, use fresh or treated medium, take cuttings only from healthy, labelled stock plants, and wash hands before handling cuttings. When cleaning with disinfectants, wear the protective equipment shown on the product label.

A supervisor checks that each propagation batch is labelled with the plant name, date and quantity, so that strike rates (the percentage that root) can be measured and improved.

lessons.title: Cultivation practices: growing on to saleable plants
lessons.html:
From young plant to finished product

Once a young plant has rooted, it must be grown on to a saleable size with good shape and health. These are the main cultivation practices you will supervise.

Potting and growing media

Young plants are transplanted into bags or pots filled with a growing medium, often a mix of composted pine bark, coir, sand or other materials. The medium must drain well and hold enough water. Plant at the same depth as before, firm gently, and water in straight after potting.

Irrigation

Water early in the day so leaves dry before night. Overhead sprinklers suit small pots in blocks; drip suits larger containers. Check that every pot is getting water, because blocked nozzles leave dry patches. Feel the weight of pots or check the medium with your finger rather than watering by habit.

Feeding

Plants are fed with slow-release fertiliser mixed into the medium, with liquid feed through the irrigation (fertigation), or both. Follow the nursery's feeding programme and the product label. Yellowing lower leaves often show nitrogen shortage; salt burn on leaf edges can mean too much feed.

Shaping and spacing

  • Pinching and pruning remove growing tips so plants become bushy rather than tall and thin.
  • Spacing pots further apart as plants grow gives light to every plant and reduces disease.
  • Staking keeps trees and climbers straight.
  • Weeding pots and paths keeps weeds from stealing water and hiding pests.

Pest and disease control

Scout plants weekly for aphids, whitefly, red spider mite, mealybug, snails and fungal spots. Use integrated pest management: good hygiene first, then biological or chemical control if needed. Only trained, authorised workers may apply agricultural remedies registered under Act 36 of 1947, always following the label and wearing the required protective clothing. Never spray in wind or near workers without protection.

Hardening off

Before sale, plants are moved to more open conditions so they can cope with full sun, wind and less frequent watering at the customer's home.

Key points

  • Plants need light, water, air, nutrients and the right temperature at every stage.
  • Seed is cheap for large numbers; vegetative methods keep plants true to type.
  • Hygiene and labelling are vital in propagation.
  • Water, feed, pinch and space plants according to the production programme.
  • Only trained workers apply agricultural remedies, following the label.
